headline: Saudi AI capacity is limited by megawatts, not by chips
deck: Operational data centre load stood near 467MW in the first quarter against pipelines quoted in gigawatts. The gap is an electrical engineering problem.
excerpt: Saudi Arabia operated around 467 megawatts of data centre load in the first quarter of 2026. The announced pipelines are an order of magnitude larger, and closing that distance is a matter of substations and connection dates rather than semiconductors.
content:
The Global AI Summit opens in Riyadh this week into a conversation that has been dominated by chips, and the Saudi constraint is not chips.

The Kingdom operated around 467 megawatts of data centre load in the first quarter of 2026, up from roughly 440 megawatts at the end of 2025. The announced pipelines are an order of magnitude larger: Humain's corporate targets run into multiple gigawatts, and the fortnight since LEAP has added several hundred megawatts of individually announced capacity from Al Moammar, NHC Innovation, stc and others.

Closing the distance between the operating figure and the announced figure is an electrical engineering programme, and it moves at the speed of the slowest item in it.

The sequence is well understood by anyone who has built one. A campus of a few hundred megawatts requires a bulk supply point at transmission voltage, which requires the network operator to have capacity at that location or to reinforce it. Reinforcement means transformers and extra-high-voltage switchgear, which are procured on lead times that have lengthened globally as every grid invests at once. Behind that sits the site's own distribution: medium-voltage switchgear, transformers, uninterruptible supplies, standby generation and the cooling plant, all of which draw on the same manufacturing base.

That is why the electricity agreements signed at LEAP mattered more than their coverage suggested. Saudi Energy signed three agreements to support digital infrastructure for data and AI centres, the first between National Grid SA and Humain covering supply to the Riyadh artificial intelligence data centres project. A signed supply agreement converts an assumption into a date, and the date is what the rest of the programme is scheduled against.

The second constraint is thermal and it is specific to this climate. Rack densities for training hardware have moved beyond what air cooling handles economically, which pushes new build towards liquid distribution to the rack. In Saudi ambient conditions, heat rejection is harder and more energy-hungry than in temperate markets, and the choice between evaporative cooling and dry coolers is a water-against-power decision made differently here than elsewhere. Evaporative systems are more efficient and consume water the Kingdom desalinates; dry coolers consume none and draw more electricity from the grid already under pressure.

None of this makes the pipeline implausible. It makes it a construction and procurement schedule rather than a technology one, and it puts the achievable rate of growth in the hands of transformer factories, electrical contractors and the transmission operator rather than in the hands of a chip supplier.

The summit runs at the King Abdulaziz International Conference Centre until 17 September.
author: Mo Qureshi
scheduledReason: Written before the Global AI Summit opens in Riyadh on 15 September. It works from the published programme, SDAIA's announcements and verified infrastructure data, and makes no claim about anything said at the event.
